## Status and sequencing

**BACKLOG — NOT ADMITTED FOR EXECUTION.** Start development **only after [Task #24](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/issues/24) is completed** and its accepted self-adoption state is reconciled. Do not allocate Step 1, launch Manual Codex, prepare an implementation PR or change active governance merely by creating this Issue. Owner will authorize execution separately after #24. This is an enhancement of the existing common **Task handoff and continuation** protocol, not a reopening of completed [Task #14](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/issues/14).

## Problem

Four shortcomings surfaced in the Task #24 work and the subsequent review of research Tasks in Codex Relay:

1. After Codex returned its Step 1 research Outcome, the next architect/owner-to-Codex execution was incorrectly called a continuation of Step 1 rather than Step 2. The current shared protocol distinguishes Step, attempt and conversation but leaves allocation to each project; the manual binding does not supply a clear definition.
2. Later owner directions were repeatedly inserted at the top of the Issue body, above older Outcomes and reviews. A human reading body then chronological comments cannot reconstruct the original charter and subsequent decisions naturally; reopening and public discussion would make this worse.
3. Manual Codex prompts repeated investigation/check lists already defined in the Issue instead of providing a small formal handoff to the canonical Task authority.
4. Relay's automatic positive exact-head PR review normally publishes `APPROVE` and permits safe authorized auto-merge. This works for ordinary implementation/fixes with previously agreed acceptance criteria, but a research, architecture or methodology result may require owner discussion **before formal approval**. The owner should not have to remember an ad hoc prohibition for every such Task. For example, [Relay Task #42](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/issues/42) produced reviewable research [PR #120](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/pull/120) and [PR #121](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/pull/121), which received formal approval and were merged while the actual app-server architecture decision remained distinct.

Use the recorded [Task #24 Step 1 Outcome](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/issues/24#issuecomment-6120052165), its later Step 2 admission, the existing shared protocol and [manual binding](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/blob/main/docs/manual-task-handoff.md) as the main failure case. [Task #14 Step 2](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/issues/14#issuecomment-6114902589) is an important positive counterexample: a new Step corrected a reviewed result while updating the same PR. [Relay #108's accepted analysis](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/blob/66870385a60a787150c9b221bf830c013b2816e7/docs/task-handoff-methodology-analysis.md) and [Relay #115's target design](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/issues/115) are comparative evidence, **not imported execution authority or a dependency on Relay automation**.

## Required shared semantics

### 1. One Step = one authorized architect/owner ↔ executor work iteration

A Step is a separately authorized **execution cycle**: the architect/owner hands a bounded Task objective to an implementer (e.g. Manual Codex), the implementer investigates/implements, tests and fixes as needed, and returns a terminal execution result (Outcome, BLOCKED, or other explicitly recognized terminal handoff) for assessment.

- The **next newly authorized execution handoff after a terminal result allocates the next Step**, even when continuing the same goal, correcting the same findings or reusing the same branch/PR. Review/Decision/discussion between Steps does not itself allocate one.
- Internal implementation/testing/corrections **before that execution hands off a terminal result** remain within its Step. Ordinary active-execution clarifications do not create a Step.
- Retry/recovery/republication of the **same** execution/result without a fresh execution cycle preserves identity; a genuinely new execution after BLOCKED gets a new Step. Do not equate Step with PR, commit, conversation, transport attempt, test pass or formal lifecycle phase.
- A completed Step does not establish Task completion. No artificial Steps merely to separate coding from testing; one admitted execution should carry its in-scope develop/test/fix cycle to a useful result.
- Keep the reusable definition independent of Codex Relay's Writer reservations, labels, native Task Request, reviewer identity or automated admission implementation. Any project-specific identity/authorization mechanism belongs in its binding; it may **implement**, but not silently redefine, these shared semantics.

### 2. Stable charter and chronologically appended authority

The Task must be understandable by reading its original charter, subsequent discussion, decisions, Outcomes and reviews **in chronological order**, without mentally relocating newer body text to later dates.

- **Before execution begins:** allow a placeholder/idea Task body to evolve into a complete actionable charter. Proportionately choose consolidation in body versus a separate Decision: consolidate when it improves clarity without hiding substantive public discussion, contribution attribution or decision provenance; preserve/link meaningful earlier discussion as appropriate. Do not demand a formal Decision for every preliminary thought or editorial refinement.
- **From first authorized execution onward:** treat body as the stable historical charter. Do not prepend or rewrite substantive scope, requirements, permissions, completion/closure rules or newly admitted work into the body after Outcomes. Record changes in **chronologically appended, explicit owner-authorized Task Decision comments** (or equivalently durable, clearly linked decision records in a non-GitHub tracker). Allow only narrowly non-semantic editorial corrections to body; never use these to obscure changed authority.
- **After completion/reopening:** preserve the original body and historical execution/acceptance; record reasons, changes and any new execution admission in subsequent chronological Decisions. Reopening does not reset Step numbering or accepted history.
- Resolve **effective current authority** from the original charter **plus applicable authorized Decisions**, including explicit supersession or revocation, not simply from the current body and not from every conversational comment. Outcomes/reviews are evidence and assessment, not automatic permission to change scope.
- A Decision should be concise and human-readable, identify what was decided, relevant prior Outcome/discussion and any resulting scope/authorization/Step direction. Distinguish changes to Task authority from PR-specific review findings/remediation. No blanket mandatory JSON/typed publication or mechanical comment for routine already-authorized actions.

### 3. Minimal formal execution handoff

The normal handoff must be a **short navigation and start instruction**, not an alternate specification. As the default, it contains only **Task, Step, short purpose, repository/canonical Task link** and a direction to resolve the full current authority (charter, chronological Decisions, relevant Outcomes/reviews and current accepted governance), execute the admitted Step and publish its result for the applicable independent assessment.

- Do **not** restate goals, individual requirements, investigation steps, test matrices or boundaries already accessible in canonical authority, even if such duplication seems helpful. The executor must read the complete relevant Issue discussion and linked records, **not just the Issue body**.
- Include only irreducible handoff-specific routing or environment facts that are not available from authority, e.g. starting worktree or a material access limitation. No universal model/effort field, extra ceremony or duplicate publication contract.
- Make the existing local Manual Codex example accurately demonstrate this strict minimal default. A new Step after Outcome uses a new small handoff and the corresponding Decision, not a rewritten charter.

Illustrative shape (not a new machine-readable schema):

```text
Task N — Step S — <purpose>
Repository: <owner/repo>
Issue: <canonical Task URL>

Read the full Task chronology, current authorized Decisions, prior results/reviews
and accepted governance. Execute the admitted Step end-to-end, publish its
attributable Outcome, and stop at the applicable independent review boundary.
```

### 4. Acceptance strategies: direct vs deliberative

This protocol should define a small, reusable **Task result acceptance strategy**: when may the reviewer publish a formal positive acceptance immediately, and when must a meaningful owner discussion/decision come **before** `APPROVE`? This choice concerns the type of **decision needed to accept the result**, not whether the Task is technically coded or documentation-only.

- **Direct acceptance (standard):** For fixes, implementation of already agreed requirements, and other work whose desired result and criteria are established. A sufficiently independent exact-result review may publish `APPROVE` directly when all applicable evidence/checks and authority requirements are satisfied. The adopting project's previously authorized post-approval continuation, including automatic safe squash merge, is unchanged.
- **Deliberative acceptance (standard):** For open research, selecting architecture, methodology/policy proposals, or other results requiring owner judgment about alternatives, trade-offs or newly proposed commitments. The reviewer first produces a substantive **non-approving assessment or preview**, including findings and warnings. Even a positive assessment must **not** publish formal `APPROVE` or trigger approval-driven merge before the owner has had the intended discussion and recorded the necessary Decision. No fake `REQUEST_CHANGES` merely to suppress auto-merge if the report has no defects.

**Selection/defaults/overrides:** Prefer (1) an explicit owner-authorized strategy in the Task charter or subsequent Task Decision, then (2) applicable adopting-project rules including additional named strategies, then (3) shared defaults: Direct when requirements/result are already decided; Deliberative when the output itself requires an architectural, methodological or policy choice. A technical research Task can be Deliberative; a correction to already accepted governance can be Direct. A strategy may be revised by an authorized Decision before acceptance. Resolve material ambiguity about the need for owner deliberation before formal `APPROVE`. Project customization cannot weaken independent assessment, accepted owner/trust boundaries or required checks.

**Deliberative lifecycle:**

1. Executor returns an attributable Outcome and reviewable immutable result. Independent evaluator performs substantive exact-result review and supplies a **non-approving** assessment/preview. Its findings and evidence may be recorded or presented via an authorized project mechanism, without issuing the final approval yet.
2. Architect/owner discusses the result and records an explicit decision: accept the result, request corrections/new work, reject the result, or accept the **quality of a research report without adopting the architecture/policy it recommends**. Do not conflate report acceptance with authorization to implement, migrate, install or release the recommendation.
3. If owner authorizes acceptance of the unchanged result, validate that the reviewed head and authority are still current; reuse already sufficient independent review evidence and publish the actual exact-result `APPROVE`. Do not demand a duplicate complete review for the same head without a reason. If the result changes, obtain fresh applicable review. Once `APPROVE` is genuinely published, existing project-specific authorized merge/continuation behavior can proceed.
4. If the owner requests material rework or a new execution after the terminal Outcome, allocate the next Step according to the shared Step rules. Ordinary discussion or preliminary review is not itself a Step.

**Important separation:** Approval of result quality, owner selection of a recommendation, PR integration, Task closure, deployment and publication are distinct permissions/events. An independent evaluator may be positive about a research report while the owner rejects its proposed solution. Acceptance strategy must therefore govern **review-verdict publication**, not merely post-approval merge.

**Adoption boundary:** This is a common methodology and reusable default, not a new universal schema, a rigid Task classifier or a replacement for product-level Reviewer/Writer. Relay already has typed Task Decisions, native `APPROVE`/CR, `continuation.hold`, and a guarded post-approval merge policy. But `continuation.hold` blocks continuation **after** approval and does not prevent an unwanted `APPROVE` from being published. Any future Relay product adaptation must honor selected strategy **before publication of the native verdict** and preserve its existing exact-head and identity/merge guarantees. Coordinate that separate consumer work against its accepted [Task #115](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/codex-relay/issues/115) state; this shared Task does not itself authorize Relay implementation, installation or changed automation.

## Deliverables and validation

- Tighten the existing **shared** `task-handoff.md` protocol while preserving its current applicability, independent review, proportionality, warnings, authority boundaries and consumer opt-in semantics. Revise `docs/manual-task-handoff.md` and other genuinely affected local guidance/examples to remove conflicting Step/body/handoff interpretations and illustrate strategy selection and pre-approval deliberation.
- Add focused, proportional semantic/behavioral checks for: backlog placeholder refined into charter; substantial pre-execution public discussion; first execution freezing charter; Outcome → Decision → new Step on same Task/PR; BLOCKED → new execution; internal test/fix iteration vs replay; review alone/no execution not incrementing Step; superseding Decisions; reopening after closure; downstream use with no Relay; and minimal prompt without copied Issue requirements.
- Add focused acceptance-strategy walks: direct fix → review/approval/authorized merge; decision-grade technical research → positive assessment but **no premature `APPROVE`**; owner accepts report quality without adopting proposed implementation; real defects → actionable findings rather than fake CRs/holds; unchanged reviewed SHA + owner Decision → approve without redundant full review; changed SHA → new review; Task-level override, project default/extension, shared default and ambiguous classification; post-approval hold alone is insufficient. Test without Relay, and describe any required future Relay-specific enforcement separately.
- Qualify compatibility with the **accepted** self-adoption implementation and versioned `org.jresearch.ai/development-governance` package **as they stand after Task #24**. Follow accepted package-versioning, source/export, non-rewrite of frozen versions and independent exact-head review rules. Preserve existing consumer authority; publication does not silently migrate Relay or other consumers.
- Document any true conflict with currently accepted shared guarantees or product-specific obligations; do not opportunistically redesign the Relay Writer/Reviewer/admission protocol, import its typed schemas, add a new Task orchestration framework or retroactively rewrite older Issues.

## Execution and completion boundary

**Dependency:** completion of Task #24, not just a candidate PR or provisional research review. This Issue stays backlog-only until a separate owner admission of its first execution Step.

Once admitted, do the entire in-scope implementation, tests, corrections and candidate publication within each allocated Step; do not split research, coding and verification into ceremonial separate Steps. Publish a reviewable exact-head result and stop for independent review. No self-approval, merge, release, downstream installation or Issue closure is authorized by this backlog Issue.

**Done when:** the accepted common protocol gives an unambiguous Step boundary, a chronologically readable charter/Decision history and a genuinely minimal handoff, plus **reusable, overrideable acceptance strategies with a pre-`APPROVE` deliberation boundary**; the local manual binding follows it; representative edge cases pass; and the changed version has independent acceptance under ordinary release/merge boundaries.

**Owner Decision — Task #26 / Step 1 execution admission (2026-10-12)**

[Task #24](https://github.com/jresearchsoftware/shared-governance/issues/24) is completed; its native producer self-adoption is accepted in source `main` at `80318d00ec14ee3bc49a1b94cbc24e859371f80f`, and development-governance `1.3.0` is published. The explicit backlog dependency in this Task is satisfied.

**Authorize Manual Codex Step 1 now** for the already-defined Task #26 scope. This is one complete execution cycle: implement the admitted shared protocol and affected local binding, qualify behavior with proportionate checks, correct in-scope defects, and publish a reviewable PR with exact-head evidence plus an attributable canonical Outcome. Use the independently accepted source-main SHA above for the applicable instruction authority; candidate instructions and generated projections remain proposal material.

This Decision changes **execution admission only**. The Issue's existing scope, completion criteria, validation cases and boundaries remain authoritative; do not rewrite or prepend the charter. Stop after the result handoff for independent exact-head assessment. This authorization does **not** permit implementer self-approval, merge, package publication, consumer/Relay migration, installed-state changes or Task closure. Any later changed scope or a fresh post-Outcome execution requires a subsequent authorized Decision and Step allocation.

title: Clarify Task Steps, Decisions, handoffs and acceptance strategies
